topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 7 is a quarter of the award. Booklet A's three practical tasks (15 marks each) open with your own readings, and each reading written to the stated places is a mark of its own; Booklet B's written papers (35 marks each) ask for tests and their results, observations in the examiners' words, the reasons for each step of a method and the precaution that matches a hazard.
mustMemorise: Read a measuring cylinder at eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus
Record every reading to the places the table asks for, keeping the trailing zero (2.40 g, not 2.4 g), with the unit in the heading
Energy in food (J per g) = rise in temperature × volume of water × 4.2 ÷ mass of food; the question prints it
Starch test: hot water kills the leaf; ethanol, warmed in hot water with no flame near, removes the chlorophyll; hot water again softens the leaf; iodine turns blue-black where there is starch
Flame colours: lithium ion crimson, sodium ion yellow-orange, potassium ion lilac, calcium ion brick red, copper(II) ion blue-green
Hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop. Oxygen: a glowing splint relights. Carbon dioxide: bubbled through limewater, it turns colourless limewater milky
Collect a gas over water when it is insoluble or only slightly soluble in water
An observation is seen, heard, felt or smelt: bubbles, colourless, disappears, heat given out. A deduction is concluded from it
notOnThisSpec: Uncertainty in a reading (plus or minus half a division) and percentage error
Flame colours of metal ions beyond the five the specification lists

sheet.howExamined: Booklet A is three practical tasks done in school, one each for Biology, Chemistry and Physics, 15 marks each. Each task opens with your own readings entered in a table to the stated precision, and those recordings earn marks of their own before any calculation. Booklet B is three 30-minute written papers of 35 marks, sat in the Summer at the same tier: a test with its result, an observation, the reason for a step, a precaution and its reason, apparatus named or labelled, and a six-mark method written in full sentences. The Summer 2019, 2021 and 2024 Chemistry and the 2021 and 2026 Biology Booklet B papers set a practical carried out here as the six-mark question.
traps: Writing 'hydrogen given off', a deduction, where an observation was asked for, or 'clear' where the word needed was colourless (Summer 2023 Booklet A Chemistry Higher Q1)
Describing hydrochloric acid as a clear solution instead of colourless, and calling a reaction exothermic as if that were something seen (Summer 2024 Booklet A Chemistry Foundation Q1)
A mass recorded to one decimal place where two were asked for, or written without its unit (Summer 2024 Booklet A Chemistry Foundation Q1; Summer 2025 Booklet A Chemistry Higher Q1)
Anhydrous magnesium sulfate described as white crystals: examiners expected a white powder (Summer 2025 Booklet A Chemistry Foundation Q1)
'Dissolves' written for 'disappears', 'heat' written alone for 'heat given out', or 'disappears' without saying what disappeared (Summer 2024 Booklet B Chemistry Foundation Q1 and Q4)
The carbon dioxide test without 'bubbled through' or without 'colourless to milky', or a splint test given for carbon dioxide (Summer 2024 Booklet B Chemistry Foundation Q3)

The leaf-test precaution given as general safety such as tying hair back, when the answer was to turn the Bunsen off; few linked yellow-brown to no photosynthesis and no starch (Summer 2024 Booklet B Biology Foundation Q2)
A reason for stirring that does not mention heat or temperature, 'accuracy' as the reason for repeating, and vague risk actions such as 'tell someone' (Summer 2023 Booklet A Biology Foundation Q1)
The percentage of the energy that was lost found instead of the percentage that heated the water (Summer 2023 Booklet A Biology Higher Q1)
An average typed as A + B ÷ 2, so the calculator divides first and the mean lands outside the readings (Summer 2024 Booklet A Biology Foundation Q1)
Meter readings not written to the decimal places the table asks for (Summer 2023 Booklet A Physics Foundation Q1)
Saying oxygen relights a lit splint, and apparatus in a gas preparation left unnamed (Summer 2023 Unit C2 Foundation Q6)
The thistle funnel called a thistle tube, a conical flask or a syringe (Summer 2025 Unit C2 Foundation Q6)

workedExamples.stem:
A student burns a 0.8 g crisp under 20 cm³ of water. The water's temperature rises from 16 °C to 41 °C.
Energy in food (J per g) = rise in temperature × volume of water × 4.2 ÷ mass of food
The packet states that the crisp contains 21 000 J per g. What percentage of this energy heated the water? Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [5]

steps.decision: The rise is the difference between the two readings.
The equation's rise × volume of water × 4.2 is the energy the water took in.

options: 1 cm³ of water has a mass of 1 g, so the volume stands for the mass of water heated
The volume of water is always 20 cm³
The 4.2 converts the volume into joules
whyMenu.explain: Heating 1 g of water by 1 °C takes 4.2 J. Each cm³ of water is 1 g, so rise × volume × 4.2 counts the joules the water took in.

steps.working: Energy per gram = 2100 ÷ 0.8 = 2625 J per g
steps.decision: Divide by the mass of the food burnt, so foods of different masses can be compared.
The part that heated the water, over the whole, times 100. The rest was lost to the air and the glass.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: 12.5% of the energy heated the water

twin.stem: A 0.5 g cracker is burnt under 20 cm³ of water, which warms from 12 °C to 35 °C. Energy in food (J per g) = rise in temperature × volume of water × 4.2 ÷ mass of food. The packet states 23 000 J per g. What percentage of this energy heated the water? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

workedExamples.stem:
A student is given a sample of compound Z, which is made of small blue crystals. She describes its appearance, carries out a flame test on it with a nichrome wire loop and concentrated hydrochloric acid, and records a blue-green flame.
Describe the appearance of Z, describe how the test is done, and name the metal ion. The acid's bottle carries warning symbols: what are they called? [6]

steps.working: Appearance: blue crystals, a crystalline solid
steps.decision: The colour and the state together: one mark for each.

steps.working: Clean the loop: dip it in concentrated hydrochloric acid and hold it in the flame until it gives no colour
steps.decision: Traces of an earlier compound would colour the flame too.

options.feedback: The acid and the flame clean the wire until it adds no colour.
Limewater tests for carbon dioxide; it does not clean a wire.
Ethanol burns with a flame of its own and would not clean the loop of metal compounds.

steps.working: Dip the loop in the acid, then in Z, and hold it at the edge of a blue Bunsen flame: blue-green
steps.decision: Read the colour against a flame that adds none of its own.

options: A blue flame adds no colour of its own to hide the result
It is the hottest part of the flame
It is the safest place to hold the loop
whyMenu.explain: A yellow safety flame would colour the result itself. The blue flame is almost colourless, so any colour you see comes from the compound.

steps.decision: Match the colour to the list and name the ion, not the metal.

steps.working: The warning symbols are hazard symbols
steps.decision: Their name is hazard symbols; each one says what the danger is.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Blue crystals; a blue-green flame: copper(II) ion, Cu²⁺; hazard symbols

twin.stem: Compound Y is a white powder. In a flame test it gives a yellow-orange flame. Name the metal ion in Y.

items.stem: Before we start: a ruler is marked in millimetres. What is the smallest length you can read on it?

options.feedback: The smallest division is the smallest step you can read.
Each centimetre is split into ten millimetre divisions, so you can read finer than 1 cm.
That is a centimetre; the millimetre marks between let you read to 1 mm.

items.stem: Which unit is used for the volume of a liquid read from a measuring cylinder?

options.feedback: Cubic centimetres; 1 cm³ is the same as 1 ml.
Grams measure mass, read on a balance.
Centimetres measure length.
In degrees Celsius, °C.
Energy is in joules; a thermometer reads how hot something is, its temperature.
Mass is measured on a balance.

items.stem: Iron filings are stirred into blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Which statement is an observation?

options.text: a brown solid forms on the iron
options.feedback: You can see the brown solid appear: an observation.

options.text: copper is displaced by the iron
options.feedback: That explains what happened: a deduction, not something seen.
The iron reacts; examiners do not accept dissolves for a reacting solid.
Clear only means see-through; a solution that loses its colour is described as colourless or paler.

items.stem: Why can hydrogen be collected over water?

options.feedback: A gas that does not dissolve bubbles up and pushes the water out of the jar.

options.text: it is less dense than air
options.feedback: Density decides upward or downward delivery through air; over water it is solubility that matters.
Flammability is a hazard and the basis of its test, not why it collects over water.

items.stem: In the test of a leaf for starch, how should the tube of ethanol be warmed?

options.text: stand it in hot water with no flame nearby
options.feedback: Ethanol is flammable, so it is warmed by hot water only.

options.text: hold it over a Bunsen flame
options.feedback: Ethanol catches fire easily; never heat it over a flame.

options.text: warm it gently at the edge of a blue flame
options.feedback: Any flame near ethanol could set it alight; hot water does the warming.

items.stem: A results table asks for masses to 2 decimal places. Which entry is written correctly?

options.feedback: Two decimal places, the trailing zero kept.
One decimal place: the zero the table asks for has been dropped.
Three decimal places: more than the table asks for.

items.stem: In a food-burning experiment, why is the water stirred before the final temperature is read?

options.text: so the heat is spread evenly and the reading is the temperature of all the water
options.feedback: Without stirring, the water nearest the flame is warmer than the rest.
Mixing is what stirring does; the mark is for why: the heat, or the temperature, spread evenly.

options.text: to help the food burn completely
options.feedback: The water does not touch the food; stirring evens out the temperature of the water.

parts.stem: The diagram shows part of a measuring cylinder holding the water for a food-burning experiment. Read the volume of water in the cylinder. Give your answer in cm³.

scheme.for: 13 cm³, read at the bottom of the meniscus (the unit in brackets carries no mark)

context.setting: Identifying a metal ion with a nichrome wire loop

parts.stem: Before a flame test, what is the nichrome wire loop dipped in to clean it?

options.feedback: Dipped in the acid and held in the flame until it adds no colour.
Sodium hydroxide would leave sodium on the wire, and sodium colours a flame yellow-orange.
Limewater is the test for carbon dioxide; it does not clean the wire.
Tap water holds dissolved salts that can colour the flame.

scheme.for: concentrated hydrochloric acid

parts.workedSolution: concentrated hydrochloric acid. Dipped in the acid and held in the flame until it adds no colour.

parts.stem: Where should the loop be held to see the flame colour?

options.text: at the edge of a blue Bunsen flame
options.feedback: A blue flame adds almost no colour of its own.
The yellow flame's own colour would hide the result.

options.text: just above the tip of the flame
options.feedback: Above the flame the loop is not hot enough to colour it.

options.text: in the air beside the burner
options.feedback: The compound must be heated in the flame to give a colour.

scheme.for: at the edge of a blue Bunsen flame

parts.workedSolution: at the edge of a blue Bunsen flame. A blue flame adds almost no colour of its own.

parts.stem: Why is the loop cleaned again before the next sample is tested?

options.text: so traces of the last compound do not colour the flame
options.feedback: Otherwise the colours of two compounds could mix.
Cleaning heats the wire in the flame; the aim is to remove old compound.
Cleaning changes nothing about the flame; it removes old compound from the wire.

options.text: to help the next solid stick to the loop
options.feedback: Dipping in the acid just before the solid helps it stick; cleaning is about removing the last compound.

scheme.for: so traces of the last compound do not colour the flame

parts.workedSolution: so traces of the last compound do not colour the flame. Otherwise the colours of two compounds could mix.

context.setting: A geranium leaf partly covered with black card

hints: Starch has to be used up before the experiment starts, and the light has to come before the test.
parts.stem: A student investigates whether light is needed for photosynthesis, using a geranium plant. Put her steps in the right order.

expectedOrder: Put the plant in a dark cupboard for two days
Cover part of one leaf with a strip of black card
Leave the plant in bright light for a day
Remove the leaf and take off the card
Test the leaf for starch with iodine solution

scheme.for: all five in order [2]; one neighbouring pair swapped [1] (the order thresholds are written here, as the spec has no thresholds field yet)

parts.workedSolution: Dark cupboard for two days; black card on part of one leaf; bright light for a day; remove the leaf and the card; test with iodine solution.

parts.stem: Why is the plant kept in the dark before the experiment?

options.text: to use up the starch already in its leaves, so any starch found was made during the experiment
options.feedback: In the dark it cannot photosynthesise, so it uses its stored starch.
The ethanol removes the chlorophyll, during the test; the dark empties the starch store.
The hot water after the ethanol softens the leaf; the dark empties the starch store.

options.text: to stop it taking in water
options.feedback: A plant in the dark still takes in water; what it cannot do is photosynthesise.

scheme.for: to use up the starch already in its leaves, so any starch found was made during the experiment

parts.workedSolution: to use up the starch already in its leaves, so any starch found was made during the experiment. In the dark it cannot photosynthesise, so it uses its stored starch.

context.setting: Sodium carbonate powder added to dilute nitric acid

hints: Write what you would see: something rising through the liquid, and something at the bottom of the tube.

commonErrors.feedback: Naming the gas, calling it exothermic or naming the reaction is a deduction. Write what you see: bubbles, the solid disappearing, a colourless solution.
The powder reacts, so it disappears; examiners do not accept dissolves for a solid that reacts with acid.

parts.stem: A small spatula of white sodium carbonate powder is added to excess dilute nitric acid in a test tube. Give two observations: one that shows a gas is made, and one about the powder.

accepted: Fizzing, and the white powder disappears
bubbles of gas are given off; the solid disappears

any: solid can no longer be seen
powder can no longer be seen

scheme.for: bubbles / fizzing / effervescence / gas given off (not the gas named: that is a deduction)
the solid (powder) disappears / gets smaller; not dissolves

parts.workedSolution: Fizzing (bubbles of gas), and the white powder disappears.

hints: Say what colour it is. See-through is not a colour.

commonErrors.feedback: Clear only means you can see through it; a blue solution is clear too. The colour word is colourless.

parts.stem: Describe the liquid left in the test tube when the reaction has stopped.

scheme.for: colourless (solution); not clear, which only means see-through

parts.workedSolution: A colourless solution.

context.setting: Three breakfast cereals burnt under a boiling tube of water

hints: Think what would change the rise in temperature apart from the cereal and the water.

commonErrors.feedback: The cereal is what she changes on purpose, so it cannot be kept the same. Give something fixed, such as the volume of water.

parts.stem: A student compares the energy in three breakfast cereals by burning a sample of each under a boiling tube of water. She keeps the volume of water the same each time. Give one other variable she must keep the same.

accepted: the distance of the food from the boiling tube

any: all of the food is burnt

scheme.for: any one from: the distance of the food from the boiling tube; each sample burnt completely [1]

parts.workedSolution: The distance of the burning food from the boiling tube (or: burning each sample completely).

hints: Which part of the water is nearest the flame?

commonErrors.feedback: Stirring does mix the water, but the mark is for why: the heat, or the temperature, is spread evenly so the reading is right for all of it.

parts.stem: Why is the water stirred before the final temperature is read?

accepted: So the heat is spread evenly and the thermometer reads the temperature of all the water

scheme.for: the heat (or the temperature) is spread evenly through the water / the water is the same temperature throughout [1]; the answer must mention heat or temperature

parts.workedSolution: So the heat is spread evenly through the water, and the thermometer reads the temperature of all of it.

context.setting: A rice cake burnt under 25 cm³ of water

commonErrors.feedback: 31 °C is the final temperature. The rise is the final temperature minus the starting one.

parts.stem: A student burns a 0.7 g rice cake under 25 cm³ of water. The temperature of the water rises from 15 °C to 31 °C. Calculate the rise in temperature, in °C.

hints: Multiply the rise by the volume of water and by 4.2, then divide by the mass of the food.

commonErrors.feedback: That puts the rice cake's mass where the volume of water goes. Multiply the rise by the 25 cm³ of water and 4.2, then divide by the food's mass.
1680 J is the energy the water took in. Per gram means dividing by the mass of the rice cake.

parts.stem:
Energy in food (J per g) = rise in temperature × volume of water × 4.2 ÷ mass of food
Use your answer to (a) to calculate the energy in the rice cake, in J per g.

scheme.for: rise (from (a)) × 25 × 4.2
÷ 0.7, the mass of the rice cake
2400 (J per g), or the value from her own rise

context.setting: A gas made in a conical flask and collected over water

parts.stem: A gas is made in a conical flask closed with a bung. Which piece of apparatus, fitted through the bung, lets the acid be added without opening the flask?

options.feedback: Its long stem goes through the bung and dips below the liquid, so gas cannot escape up it.
The delivery tube carries the gas away to the jar; the acid goes in through the thistle funnel.
A gas syringe collects and measures gas; the acid goes in through a thistle funnel.
The beehive shelf holds the gas jar in the trough, at the other end of the apparatus.

scheme.for: a thistle funnel

parts.workedSolution: a thistle funnel. Its long stem goes through the bung and dips below the liquid, so gas cannot escape up it.

parts.stem: The first gas jar collected is often thrown away. Suggest why.

options.text: it is mostly air pushed out of the flask and tubes
options.feedback: The gas made first pushes the air ahead of it into the jar.

options.text: the first gas made is impure because the acid is cold
options.feedback: The gas itself is the same all the way through; the first jar holds the air it pushed out.

options.text: the gas jar was not full of water
options.feedback: The jar starts full of water; the first gas to arrive is the air from the flask.

options.text: the first gas is too hot to test
options.feedback: It is not the temperature; the first jar holds the air that was in the flask and tubes.

scheme.for: it is mostly air pushed out of the flask and tubes

parts.workedSolution: it is mostly air pushed out of the flask and tubes. The gas made first pushes the air ahead of it into the jar.

context.setting: Yeast fermenting sugar in a flask with a delivery tube

hints: Name the solution, then say what it looks like before and after the gas passes through it.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the test for a different gas: a splint test is for hydrogen or oxygen. Carbon dioxide turns colourless limewater milky.
Limewater is right. The result needs both halves: the limewater starts colourless and turns milky.

parts.stem: Yeast is fermenting sugar solution in a flask, and the gas it gives off passes out along a delivery tube. Describe how to show that the gas is carbon dioxide, and give the result.

accepted: Bubble the gas through limewater; the colourless limewater turns milky

scheme.for: limewater (calcium hydroxide solution), the gas bubbled through it
colourless (at the start), not clear
turns milky / a white precipitate forms

parts.workedSolution: Bubble the gas through limewater: the colourless limewater turns milky.

context.setting: Zinc granules reacting with dilute sulfuric acid

parts.stem: Zinc granules are added to dilute sulfuric acid. "Bubbles rise from the surface of the zinc." Is this an observation or a deduction?

options.feedback: you can watch the bubbles rise.
It can be seen: you can watch the bubbles rise.

scheme.for: an observation

parts.workedSolution: an observation. you can watch the bubbles rise.

parts.stem: "Zinc is more reactive than hydrogen." Is this an observation or a deduction?

options.feedback: It is not something seen: it is a conclusion drawn from the bubbling.
it is a conclusion drawn from the bubbling.

scheme.for: a deduction

parts.workedSolution: a deduction. it is a conclusion drawn from the bubbling.

parts.stem: "The zinc granules get smaller." Is this an observation or a deduction?

options.feedback: you can see the granules shrink.
It can be seen: you can see the granules shrink.

scheme.for: an observation

parts.workedSolution: an observation. you can see the granules shrink.

parts.stem: "Hydrogen gas is given off." Is this an observation or a deduction?

options.feedback: It is not something seen: nobody can see which gas it is; only a test shows it.
nobody can see which gas it is; only a test shows it.

scheme.for: a deduction

parts.workedSolution: a deduction. nobody can see which gas it is; only a test shows it.

context.setting: A destarched leaf partly covered with black card

hints: Link three things: what the card did, what the leaf could not do, and what it could not make.

commonErrors.feedback: The covered part stays yellow-brown: blue-black shows starch, and no starch was made where no light reached.

parts.stem: A destarched plant has part of one leaf covered with black card, and is then left in bright light for a day. When the leaf is tested with iodine solution, the part that was covered stays yellow-brown. Explain this result.

accepted: The card kept the light out, so that part could not photosynthesise, so no starch was made there

scheme.for: no light reached the covered part (the card blocks the light)
so no photosynthesis there
so no starch made, and iodine stays yellow-brown

parts.workedSolution: The card kept the light out, so that part of the leaf could not photosynthesise, so no starch was made there and the iodine stayed yellow-brown.

parts.stem:
A student burns a crisp under a boiling tube of water, set up as shown, to find how much energy it contains.
Describe how she should carry out the experiment, from the first reading to the calculation, and suggest two reasons why her result is lower than the energy the crisp really contains.
Your written communication is marked here too: answer in full sentences, in a sensible order, using the correct scientific terms. [6]

bands.descriptor: At least five of the indicative points, including at least one reason the value is low, in a sensible order; specialist terms used accurately; at least one sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, and the meaning is always clear.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist terms; the meaning can be followed.
One or two of the indicative points; few specialist terms; the meaning may be unclear in places.

indicativeContent.point: weigh the crisp on a balance
measure a set volume of water into the boiling tube with a measuring cylinder
record the starting temperature of the water
light the crisp in the Bunsen flame and hold it just under the boiling tube
let it burn completely, relighting it if it goes out
stir the water and record the final (highest) temperature
work out the rise and the energy per gram: rise × volume × 4.2 ÷ mass
reason: heat is lost to the air, the surroundings
reason: heat warms the boiling tube, the glass and the thermometer
reason: the crisp does not burn completely

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place the answer within its band on the quality of the writing. Band A [5]–[6] at least five points including a reason the value is low; band B [3]–[4] three or four; band C [1]–[2] one or two; [0] nothing worthy of credit. A Biology answer needs at least one sentence with a capital letter and a full stop.

parts.workedSolution: First she weighs the crisp on a balance. She measures 20 cm³ of water into the boiling tube with a measuring cylinder and records its starting temperature. She lights the crisp in the Bunsen flame, holds it just under the boiling tube and lets it burn completely, relighting it if it goes out. She stirs the water and records the final temperature, then works out the rise and the energy per gram: rise × volume of water × 4.2 ÷ mass of the crisp. The value is lower than the true one because much of the heat is lost to the surrounding air, and some warms the boiling tube and the thermometer rather than the water.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'Her measured value is 2310 J per g, and the packet states 16 500 J per g. What percentage of the packet's energy heated the water? [3]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Energy on the packet = 16 500 J per g
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right. Line 3 finds the part that was lost to the air and the glass, not the part that heated the water. The question asks for the measured energy over the packet's: 2310 ÷ 16 500 × 100 = 14%.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of three: the method of a percentage stands, but it is the wrong percentage. Summer 2023 Booklet A examiners saw a few find the heat lost instead.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ryan is asked: 'Two groups burn the same food. Group 1's water rises by 26 °C and group 2's by 30 °C. Calculate the mean rise. [2]'
His answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The calculator divided only 30 by 2 before adding, because division comes first. A mean of 41 °C is bigger than both readings, which should have looked wrong. Add first in brackets: (26 + 30) ÷ 2 = 28 °C.
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks: the value is wrong and the working shows no correct sum. Summer 2024 Booklet A examiners saw averages entered as A + B ÷ 2 in exactly this way.

findings.wentWrong: Most earned both marks; the marks that went were for a mass written to one decimal place and for a mass with no unit.

findings.rule: Weigh inside the range asked, then write every reading to 2 d.p. (2.30 g, not 2.3 g).

findings.wentWrong: Most wrote current to two decimal places and voltage to one, as the table asked; weaker candidates ignored the decimal places and lost the marks.
findings.rule: Read each meter to the decimal places the table heading asks for, keeping the trailing zero (0.40 A).

findings.wentWrong: Most completed the table well; the errors were a deduction written where an observation was asked (hydrogen given off) and 'clear' written for a liquid that had to be called colourless.
findings.rule: Write what you see (bubbles, the solid disappears, a colourless solution), never what you conclude from it.

insight.ruleToRemember: Read every instrument to the precision it shows or the table asks for, keep the trailing zero and the unit, weigh within the range the task sets, and record what you see rather than what you conclude.
